comments.author: stcredzero
comments.story: U.S. Warns Of Spy Dangers Of Chinese-Made Drones
comments.why: Shows expensive security cameras had very poor security.
comments.text: These vague "The Chinese are up to something but we cannot reveal what" isn't really helpful, particularly given the current trade tensions This is exacerbated by the very poor levels of security in these devices in general: DEF CON 23 - Robinson and Mitchell - Knocking my neighbors kids cruddy drone offline [LINK] However, to put things into perspective, purpose built security cameras -- even expensive ones from well reputed industry brands -- have had similar very poor levels of very poor security for many years. [VIDEO] It's not really a problem of drones. It's a problem with the poor levels of security in consumer devices in general. It's "as if" the situation has been engineered to let bad actors do lots of spying.

comments.author: runlevel1
comments.story: The Big Hack: Statements From Amazon, Apple, Supermicro, Chinese Government
comments.why: Shows similar vendor firmware insecurity in webcams.
comments.text: Most of the out-of-band management systems (aka IPMI/DRAC/LOM) that server vendors use are built by the same 2-3 companies and rebranded. These companies churn out some truly horrible software with little consideration for security. It's often difficult to automate firmware updates, so they tend to stay vulnerable. It's a similar situation to webcams: [VIDEO]

comments.author: dralley
comments.story: Zero-Day Bug Allows Hackers to Access CCTV Surveillance Cameras
comments.why: Illustrates poor security of surveillance cameras.
comments.text: Ah, security cameras. Never-updated linux boxes, frequently with homegrown http servers, often with secret hardcoded credentials in clear text laying around in the firmware blob. [VIDEO]
